References / Signage / 139

China Club sign and invitation

April Greiman’s identity for the China Club restaurant in Los Angeles: a round neon sign with spaced, doubled letters, and a tilted opening invitation with rules, triangles, and a squiggle.

Source
People’s Graphic Design Archive: Signage for China Club
Creator
April Greiman
Made
1980 (invitation dated by the People’s Graphic Design Archive; the sign is undated there)
Style
New Wave typography (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Kinetic, playful, layered, nocturnal

Inspected two People’s Graphic Design Archive images: a night photograph of the sign (1118 × 1098) and a photograph of the opened invitation (item 1819, 970 × 1452). Not stored. The owners of the physical objects are not stated.

Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The People’s Graphic Design Archive credits the sign and the invitation to April Greiman for the China Club, California, and dates the invitation 1980. Sign, invitation.

The invitation lists April Greiman and Jayme Odgers among the credits and gives the address 8338 W Third Street, Los Angeles.

Observed

  • The sign is a black disc on a pale wall, with two dark bars behind it at an angle.
  • “CHINA” and “CLUB” are white neon capitals with wide spaces between the letters, set on a rising diagonal. A blue copy of each letter sits slightly offset behind it.
  • A red and yellow neon squiggle rises from the top left edge of the disc.
  • The invitation is a folded card with a trapezoid outline, black above and red below.
  • On the invitation, event details sit on thin parallel rules that tilt; the year is set as “1 9 8 0” with wide spaces. The credits on the red half run upside down along diagonal rules.
  • White triangles, round punched holes, a thin wavy line, and short rules are scattered over both halves.

Why it belongs

The offset blue copy in the neon is the sign-maker’s version of an overprint: two film layers that do not quite register. The invitation uses tilted rules as a staff for spaced type, as in Weingart’s covers.

Borrow

Set a short name in spaced capitals on a diagonal, with an offset second colour behind it.

Put event details on tilted hairline rules instead of a straight list.

Use one free squiggle as a counterpoint to straight bars.
